p.src: Why the Apparatus Cannot Be Removed

u.src: Why the Apparatus Cannot Be Removed
en: Why the Apparatus Cannot Be Removed

p.src: Classical mechanics encourages us to imagine an ideal observer who learns about a system while disturbing it as little as desired. Suppose, for example, that we want to see a macroscopic object. We illuminate it, collect the reflected light with a lens, and amplify the image. The light exerts some force, but in the classical idealization its intensity can be reduced while the amplification is increased. The disturbance can be made arbitrarily small without abandoning the idea of a measurement.

p.src: That limiting procedure fails in quantum mechanics. An apparatus can be improved, shielded, and calibrated, but a measurement cannot in general be made both informative and arbitrarily noninvasive. Something about the system changes. This does not mean that every measurement destroys every property or that the outcome cannot be reproduced. It means that the apparatus is part of the physical question being asked, and the state after the measurement cannot be ignored.

p.src: Now turn the apparatus through $180^\circ$. A spin that gave $+1$ with the upward orientation gives $-1$ with the inverted orientation. Turn the apparatus upright again and the result is $+1$. Orientation therefore matters. A thermometer would not report minus the temperature merely because it was turned upside down; the spin analyzer behaves differently because it asks a directional question.

p.src: Prepare a spin by obtaining $\sigma_z=+1$, and then measure $\sigma_x$. Half the identically prepared trials give $+1$, and half give $-1$. Thus $\langle \sigma_x\rangle=0.$ The same preparation gives $\langle \sigma_y\rangle=0.$ Conversely, a spin prepared with $\sigma_x=+1$ has equal probabilities for the two outcomes of a subsequent $z$- or $y$-measurement.

p.src: Classical Propositions as Sets

u.src: Classical Propositions as Sets
en: Classical Propositions as Sets

p.src: Before constructing the quantum state space, consider how logic works for a classical system. Let the possible states form a set $\Omega$. A proposition $A$ is represented by the subset of states for which $A$ is true.

u.src: Before constructing the quantum state space, consider how logic works for a classical system. Let the possible states form a set $\Omega$. A proposition $A$ is represented by the subset of states for which $A$ is true.
en: Before constructing the quantum state space, consider how logic works for a classical system. Let the possible states form a set $\Omega$. A proposition $A$ is represented by the subset of states for which $A$ is true.

p.src:
For a six-sided die, $A=\{2,4,6\}$ may represent the result is even, while $B=\{4,5,6\}$ may represent the result is greater than three. Logical operations become set operations: $\neg A=A^c,\qquad
A\land B=A\cap B,\qquad
A\lor B=A\cup B.$ Here $\lor$ is the inclusive OR: $A\lor B$ is true when $A$ is true, $B$ is true, or both are true. It is not the exclusive everyday use of either $A$ or $B$, but not both.

p.src: The Linear State Space

u.src: The Linear State Space
en: The Linear State Space

p.src: A set contains elements, but there is generally no natural way to add two elements and obtain a third. A linear vector space has more structure. If $\ket{A}$ and $\ket{B}$ are vectors and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$, then $\alpha\ket{A}+\beta\ket{B}$ is another vector in the same space. Quantum states are represented in such a complex linear space.

p.src: The state space of one spin is postulated to be a two-dimensional complex vector space, $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{spin}}\cong\mathbb C^2.$ There are continuously many possible state vectors, but only two independent basis vectors are required to express any of them.

Every spin state can then be written $\ket{A}=\alpha_u\ket{u}+\alpha_d\ket{d},
\qquad \alpha_u,\alpha_d\in\mathbb C.$ The probability rule is $P(u|A)=|\alpha_u|^2,\qquad
P(d|A)=|\alpha_d|^2.$ Because one of the two outcomes must occur, $|\alpha_u|^2+|\alpha_d|^2=1.$

p.src:
Orient the apparatus along $y$, perpendicular to the board. Write $\ket{i}\longleftrightarrow\sigma_y=+1,\qquad
\ket{o}\longleftrightarrow\sigma_y=-1,$ where the ket label $i$ means in and the unadorned $i$ multiplying a ket remains the imaginary unit.

p.src:
Equal probabilities for up and down require equal coefficient magnitudes. Orthogonality between in and out requires a relative phase that makes their overlap vanish. A symmetric choice is $\begin{aligned}
\ket{i}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{u}+i\ket{d}\bigr),\\
\ket{o}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{u}-i\ket{d}\bigr).
\end{aligned}$ In the $(u,d)$ basis, all six states are $\begin{aligned}
\ket{u}&=\binom10,
&
\ket{d}&=\binom01,
\\
\ket{r}&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\binom11,
&
\ket{l}&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\binom1{-1},
\\
\ket{i}&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\binom1{i},
&
\ket{o}&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\binom1{-i}.\end{aligned}$

p.src: Why There Are Three Distinguished Basis Pairs

u.src: Why There Are Three Distinguished Basis Pairs
en: Why There Are Three Distinguished Basis Pairs

p.src: This connection can be seen by counting physical parameters. A general column $\binom{\alpha_u}{\alpha_d}$ contains two complex numbers, hence four real numbers. Normalization removes one: $|\alpha_u|^2+|\alpha_d|^2=1.$ Multiplying both entries by a common phase changes no measurement probability: $\ket{A}\sim e^{i\chi}\ket{A}.$ That removes one more real parameter. Therefore $4-1-1=2$ physical real parameters remain, exactly the number of angles needed to specify a direction in three-dimensional space.

p.src: Orthogonality Is Not Spatial Perpendicularity

u.src: Orthogonality Is Not Spatial Perpendicularity
en: Orthogonality Is Not Spatial Perpendicularity

p.src: The word orthogonal now carries an abstract, operational meaning. It must not be confused with the angle between two arrows drawn in ordinary space. The spatial directions up and down are opposite, yet the state vectors $\ket{u}$ and $\ket{d}$ are orthogonal. The spatial directions up and right are perpendicular, yet $\braket{u}{r}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\ne0.$

p.src: The same idea has a classical probabilistic analogue. Two probability distributions with disjoint support are perfectly distinguishable: an observed result identifies which distribution was used. Distributions with overlapping support cannot be distinguished without error from one sample. Quantum orthogonality plays the role of nonoverlap, while a nonzero inner product signals that some outcomes are compatible with either preparation.

p.src: The construction has so far proceeded by fitting vectors to operational facts. The three apparatus orientations label three pairs of normalized states, and the overlaps reproduce the observed probabilities. A rigorous treatment must still say how an observable such as $\sigma_z$ acts on a state and why its possible outcomes are its eigenvalues. That is the next step.

p.src: The earlier logical puzzle can now be stated more sharply. Propositions correspond to subspaces or their projectors, and incompatible projectors do not commute. The order-sensitive OR test was not a verbal paradox; it was an early appearance of this noncommutative structure.

p.src: Finally, a measurement should not be pictured as merely uncovering a value that the spin carried in the classical sense all along. It prepares the state associated with the recorded result. An immediate repetition of the same measurement is therefore consistent, while a new ensemble of identically prepared spins displays the probability distribution dictated by the relevant amplitudes. The mathematical description of that preparation and readout will become precise once observables are introduced as operators.
